name: Poe's Law
statement: Without a clear signal of intent, a sincere expression of extremism is indistinguishable from a parody of it.
statementAccent: indistinguishable from a parody of it
meaning: Online, with no wink to mark the joke, a genuine extreme view and a parody exaggerating that view land in exactly the same words — and at least some readers will take the parody as sincere, or the sincere post as parody.
mechanism: Text online strips out the tone, facial expression, and body language that mark irony in person. When the genuine views in a space are already extreme, a parody that exaggerates them has nowhere further to go — it occupies the same textual territory as the real thing. The only reliable fix is an explicit intent-signal: Poe's original 'winking smiley', or the modern '/s' sarcasm tag and tone indicators.

examples.text: Coined about parodies of creationists, the law now covers any hot-button extreme — atheism, capitalism, communism, feminism — where satire and sincere zeal read identically without a cue to tell them apart.
It runs both ways: genuinely extreme statements are often so over-the-top that people assume they must be parody. Sincerity gets mistaken for satire as readily as satire gets mistaken for sincerity.
The tools that defuse the law — the winking emoticon, the '/s' tag, explicit tone indicators — exist precisely because plain text cannot carry the wink on its own.

variants.name: Poe's corollary
variants.text: Genuine fundamentalist or extreme statements can be so extreme that they are mistaken for parody — the reverse direction of the law.

variants.name: Poe's paradox
variants.text: In a community of extreme views, members may start suspecting and rejecting genuine newcomers as parodists, unable to tell sincere from satirical.

variants.name: Tone indicators (the fix)
variants.text: The '/s' sarcasm tag and the broader set of tone indicators are the modern intent-signals that resolve the ambiguity Poe's Law names.

whyItMatters: It explains a structural feature of online discourse: sincerity and satire are not reliably separable in text, so irony needs to be marked, and 'it was obviously a joke' is not a safe assumption. It shapes how moderation, comedy, and propaganda all operate on the internet.

working.text: if you are being satirical about an extreme view, mark it — an emoticon, a '/s', an explicit note — because the text alone will not carry the wink.

working.lead: Don't infer intent from text alone
working.text: resist reading a post as 'obviously a joke' or 'obviously serious'; without a cue, you genuinely cannot tell, and confident guesses misfire.

working.lead: Assume some readers will take it straight
working.text: a parody of an extreme position will be read as sincere by part of your audience — plan communication and moderation around that certainty.

limits: The law is narrow: it is about online communication of extreme views, not all statements, and its failure mode is specifically the absence of intent cues. It has a dark side as a refuge — a genuinely unacceptable belief can be camouflaged as 'just irony' when challenged, which the law's ambiguity enables. And it is easily misused in reverse, dismissing a sincere but unusual view with 'that must be a Poe' to deny that anyone really holds the position.
misreadings: It is not a claim that you can never tell a joke online, nor that all extreme statements are parody. It is the narrower point that, absent a signal of intent, sincere extremism and its parody are textually indistinguishable — which is why marking intent matters.
origin: Coined by Nathan Poe on 11 August 2005, in a creationism-versus-evolution thread on the christianforums.com discussion board. His wording: 'Without a winking smiley or other blatant display of humor, it is utterly impossible to parody a Creationist in such a way that someone won't mistake for the genuine article.' It generalised from creationism to all extremism, and has a documented precedent in Jerry Schwarz's 1983 Usenet observation that, without voice inflection and body language, such messages are easily misinterpreted.

sources.text: Poe's law, Wikipedia. — the origin, the Schwarz 1983 precedent, the generalisation, and the criticism.
"Poe's Law." Know Your Meme. — the 11 August 2005 thread, the original wording, and the corollary and paradox.
